items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got a call from Count Basie, because they wanted – Joe Newman was in the band... That’s when he asked me to join the band, in 1954.

ctx.x: So in high school, then, you were playing in the band and you were – what happened when you graduated? What did you decide to do?

I started playing with – I got a call to go out. I played with several bands in Philadelphia at the same time I was in school. I played with Jimmy Gorham’s band. The first band, oddly enough – I played with a man called King Coleman. He was a friend of my father’s. He was a pianist. He had a little society group. It wasn’t a band. It was a group. He gave me the first chance to start trying to play and trying to learn to improvise, which was – I didn’t really understand, but I could read some of the melodic lines.…

and they wanted me to join that band. I quit the other band and joined them. My father said, “Yeah, but you’re not going to make any money over there, playing with Jimmy Gorham. You’re working with Mr. Sadler, and he pays you well” and so on and so on. “No, that’s not the thing to do. That’s not hep enough for me.” I had to go with this other band. So I played with them for a while. Then I finished with them, and I played with a band called the Harlem Dictators. There was a fine trumpet player in there, Frank…

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: I went with Count Basie... that’s how I came to join the band... I played in Birdland with Count Basie

ctx.x: Did you have an opportunity to go overseas a lot?
Not during that time. I never went overseas until 1954 and I went with Count Basie. That was the first time.
How did the gig with Basie come about? It’s usually word of mouth, isn’t it, that leads somewhere?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: I loved Basie’s band... I didn’t stay with them long, I wasn’t with them very long, but I enjoyed all the time that I was with them.

ctx.x: Where is the state of — I’m not sure how to ask this question, but over the years, has the way the business been set up provided you with some kind of retirement? For twenty years from now when you stop playing.

Well I get a pension from the Federation, the American Federation of Musicians. And having worked in the theater and done those jobs from which money was extracted for your pension, I’m in pretty good shape. Unfortunately when you look back and you look at Duke Ellington’s band, Woody Herman’s band, Count Basie’s band, those fellas had absolutely nothing going into a pension fund. They had nothing going in there, so that when they finished playing, it was like if they hadn’t saved any money on their own, that was…
when you’re younger, we all had the idea that this goes on forever. I mean you never look into the future, you don’t think that way, you have no reason to. But I’m one of the fortunate guys, really.

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: That was his great contribution as a bandleader in that band.

ctx.x: What was he like as a leader, in terms of how did he inspire the band? What was it that he . . . ?

He knew – he had a definite way that he liked to hear the music played. Sometimes an arranger might bring in something like Li’l Darlin’. I wasn’t there when they did the initial thing, but that was – I think Neal Hefti wrote it. It was originally [Wilder sings the melody at a brisk tempo]. It was Count who, after they had run it over a few times, thought, I think it would sound better slow. He got it down to that [Wilder sings it at the familiar languid tempo], and it became – it just became a completely
different thing, with all that soul in it. That was typical of him. He had a tremendous sense of tempo and feel for those things. That was his great contribution as a bandleader in that band.
